verdict.failure_analysis: All three trials passed all 11 hidden cases, so there were no failed hidden cases to attribute to documentation gaps. The docs did well on the exact conceptual risks this task exercises: the WP_HTML_Processor overview recommends scanning a region before editing its opener with a bookmark, next_token(), seek(), and a clean-scan check; the direct-children recipe states the #tag + non-closer + depth == container_depth + 1 pattern; next_tag() explains scanning for multiple possible tag names by walking any tag and branching on get_tag(); get_current_depth() explains why subtree guards must use >= and why closers report parent depth; create_fragment() explains null creation and later unsupported-markup detection via get_last_error(); paused_at_incomplete_token() explains checking truncation after draining the relevant scan; get_updated_html() is clearly documented as the right output API after queued edits. Near-misses were small and did not cause failures: some trials added redundant opener checks after plain next_tag(), one ignored set_bookmark()'s boolean until seek(), and one did not release a bookmark explicitly.

doc_gaps.problem: The docs state that plain next_tag() skips closers by default, but this is buried inside the query parameter table. Two trials still guarded against closers after a plain next_tag() call.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Surface the default opener-only behavior in the method summary or first example, and reserve is_tag_closer() examples for calls that opt into tag_closers => 'visit'.

doc_gaps.problem: Candidates varied on bookmark cleanup and one did not check set_bookmark() immediately. The docs say to release bookmarks, but the fail-closed early-return pattern is not made explicit at the method level.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a short general pattern showing set_bookmark() checked before a forward scan, seek() checked before mutation, and release_bookmark() in cleanup when the processor continues to be used.

doc_gaps.problem: The rendered overview has an excellent direct-child checklist, but users who land directly on method docs may not see the compact child-opener predicate.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Cross-link the direct-child opener checklist from both get_current_depth() and next_token(), emphasizing that depth alone is insufficient without token type and non-closer checks.

verdict.failure_analysis: All trials passed all hidden cases. verdict.failure_analysis: No hidden/frozen case failed across the three trials: each execution.json reports 7/7 passing cases and no _doing_it_wrong or trigger_error records. The docs did well by clearly steering subjects to WP_HTML_Processor for structural work, body fragments via create_fragment(), token walking via next_token(), subtree bounds via get_current_depth() with >=, and decoded ordinary text via get_token_type() === '#text' plus get_modifiable_text(). The implied-heading-close case was also supported by the next_token() documentation explaining that the HTML Processor visits closers for implicitly closed elements. The main near-miss is conceptual rather than functional: two trials used nested next_token() loops for repeated extraction even though the docs warn that a single cursor can make nested walks skip boundaries. The examples contain both single-subtree bounded walks and a single-loop repeated-region state machine, but the safe boundary between those patterns could be sharper.

doc_gaps.problem: The docs warn against nested next_token() loops for repeated regions, but nearby examples also show bounded subtree walks. Subjects can blur when an inner walk is acceptable and when it risks skipping the next region boundary.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a short 'repeated subtree extraction' note contrasting valid patterns: use next_tag() to find each opener followed by a bounded inner subtree walk, or use one next_token() loop with explicit state; avoid an outer next_token() loop whose inner scan consumes a boundary the outer loop still expects to handle.

doc_gaps.problem: The depth contract is documented thoroughly, but the examples focus on explicit nesting. The important behavior for malformed/common HTML is that implicitly closed elements also produce virtual closers that end a depth-bounded walk.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a generic example of an element implicitly closed by a later sibling, showing the virtual closer's lower depth and explaining that this is reliable for tree boundaries but not proof that source bytes were complete.

doc_gaps.problem: The docs explain decoded text and special-element exceptions, but the common 'text content' contract could be easier to apply if it explicitly stated that concatenating #text tokens preserves source whitespace and does not synthesize spaces around inline markup.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add one sentence to the subtree text recipe: ordinary text extraction concatenates decoded #text tokens exactly as parsed; it does not insert separator spaces for tags, and any whitespace normalization is a caller-level policy.

doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a note near get_last_error() or the mutation workflow stating how callers should treat queued mutations when `get_last_error()` is non-null, and when `paused_at_incomplete_token()` should influence whether to return modified HTML or a fallback.

trials.notes: Passed 8/8 with no _doing_it_wrong records. Correctly used WP_HTML_Processor::create_fragment(), found the first TABLE, walked tokens in one depth-bounded loop, collected only #text tokens with get_modifiable_text(), and relied on documented virtual closers for omitted TD/TR tags.

Passed 8/8 with no _doing_it_wrong records. All HTML API methods used are documented. The solution closely follows the documented subtree text-walk pattern: HTML Processor, next_tag() for TABLE, next_token(), get_current_depth(), get_token_type(), get_tag(), is_tag_closer(), and decoded get_modifiable_text().

Passed 8/8 with no _doing_it_wrong records. Correct processor and documented API use. Slightly less idiomatic than trials 1-2 because it manually scans for TABLE with next_token() instead of next_tag('TABLE') and has redundant post-loop flush logic; class_exists() is a PHP builtin, not hallucinated HTML API usage.

verdict.failure_analysis: No failed hidden cases across the three trials; every execution.json reports 8/8 passing and no _doing_it_wrong entries. The docs did well in the exact areas this task needed: html-tag-processor.md / 'Which processor should I use?' steers structural text extraction to WP_HTML_Processor; html-processor.md / next_token() explains that the HTML Processor visits implicit and end-of-input closers and synthesized table structure such as TBODY; get_current_depth() documents the >= subtree guard and the '< recorded depth' break condition; get_modifiable_text() states that #text content is already decoded and should be read only after checking get_token_type() === '#text'. Near-misses were minor: none of the trials checked paused_at_incomplete_token() or get_last_error(), but this read-only extraction task did not require rejecting truncated or unsupported input, and the docs frame those checks as needed when complete-source correctness matters.

doc_gaps.problem: The docs mention synthesized TBODY and reliable implicit closers, but do not show the token order for omitted table cell and row end tags.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a small generic trace showing that omitted TD/TR end tags produce virtual closing tokens before the next cell, row, or table boundary, so closer-driven state machines can flush repeated regions reliably.

doc_gaps.problem: The factory docs explain BODY fragment context, while the browser-style table normalization guarantee is described later under next_token().
doc_gaps.suggestion: Cross-link create_fragment() to the structural guarantees in next_token(), noting that BODY fragments containing tables are parsed with browser-style implied table structure.

trials.notes: Used the correct `WP_HTML_Processor::create_fragment()` path, walked tokens, gated on `#text`, compared decoded `get_modifiable_text()`, and emitted normalized wrappers with `serialize_token()`. All API calls are documented and no `_doing_it_wrong` records appeared. Minor concern: raw-input fallback on processor errors is a clear policy, but not normalized output.

Correct processor and core rewrite pattern. All called methods are documented, including `normalize()`. It omits the documented post-scan `get_last_error()` check, so unsupported markup after earlier emitted tokens would return a partial rewrite rather than a deliberate fallback.

Correct processor, documented methods only, idiomatic token loop, decoded text comparison, `serialize_token()` wrapping, and post-scan `get_last_error()` fallback. Minor residual concern is that the ultimate fallback can still become raw input, which is not normalized.

verdict.failure_analysis: No failed hidden cases across trials: every `execution.json` reports 8/8 passing and no `_doing_it_wrong` entries. The docs did well in the exact areas this task stresses: the processor-choice guidance says to use the HTML Processor for normalized output and implied/missing closing tags; the DOM-style text recipe says ordinary text is only `#text` tokens; `get_modifiable_text()` explains decoded text and special-element opener text; and `serialize_token()` explicitly documents token-by-token normalized rewrites with wrapper markup. The main near-miss is Trial 2's missing `get_last_error()` check, despite the `serialize_token()` section saying to reject or fall back on parser aborts. Trials 1 and 3 chose raw-input fallbacks on hard errors; the docs warn this discards rewrites and is not normalized, but leave the fallback policy to the caller contract.

doc_gaps.problem: The docs warn that raw input and `normalize($html)` discard emitted rewrites, but examples still leave fallback policy open enough that candidates may return raw HTML from functions promising normalized output.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a contract-oriented note: when a caller promises normalized HTML, raw input is not an equivalent fallback; choose an explicit sentinel, accumulated best-effort serialization, or a documented normalized-only fallback.

doc_gaps.problem: A candidate can follow the main loop pattern and still omit the post-loop parser-abort check.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Make every token-rewrite example include the small post-loop `get_last_error()` branch, or label omitted error handling as intentionally elided.

doc_gaps.problem: Decoded/raw behavior is described, but the method covers several token categories with different semantics, which is easy to misuse as a text-node predicate.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a compact token-type table directly in the method docblock: `#text` decoded ordinary text, comments raw/non-DOM text, TITLE/TEXTAREA decoded opener-carried text, SCRIPT/STYLE raw opener-carried text.

trials.notes: Correctly used WP_HTML_Tag_Processor for a flat tag scan and class edit. All calls are documented: constructor, next_tag(), set_bookmark(), seek(), add_class(), release_bookmark(), and get_updated_html(). The repeated literal bookmark is exactly the documented idiom for remembering the last match.

Correct processor choice and fully documented API usage. The found flag plus repeated set_bookmark('last-h2') is idiomatic, and add_class() correctly handles both missing and existing class attributes before get_updated_html().

Canonical-style use of the documented bookmark pattern: scan H2 tags, move the same bookmark on each match, guard with has_bookmark(), seek back, add_class(), release, and return get_updated_html(). No undocumented calls or misuse.

verdict.failure_analysis: All three trials passed all six hidden cases, with no _doing_it_wrong records. The docs supported the successful implementations well: the Tag Processor overview says to use it for flat, position-based tag and class edits; next_tag() documents string and array tag-name queries, ASCII case-insensitive matching, and that tag-like text inside comments is not matched; the bookmark section explicitly describes re-setting the same named bookmark to remember the last matching tag; add_class() documents creating/appending classes; and get_updated_html() is identified as the correct way to retrieve queued class edits. Near-misses were minor: candidates relied on external flags or has_bookmark() interchangeably, and none needed to reason about decoded text or attribute null/true/empty-string semantics because this task only edits classes on tag openers.

doc_gaps.problem: The successful path is documented, but callers still have to infer the simplest guard pattern for optional matches: external boolean versus has_bookmark() before seek().
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a short note that after a scan where a bookmark may or may not have been set, has_bookmark() is the direct way to test whether seek() is meaningful; an external found flag is also fine when it is tied to successful matches.

doc_gaps.problem: The docs correctly say false can mean no match or incomplete trailing syntax, but they do not spell out how this affects already-bookmarked earlier complete tags for simple mutation tasks.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Clarify that complete tokens matched before an incomplete trailing token remain valid for queued edits/bookmarks, while callers whose contract requires complete input should check paused_at_incomplete_token() before applying results.

trials.notes: Used the correct WP_HTML_Tag_Processor for a flat attribute edit, called only documented APIs, walked tags with next_tag(), removed names returned by get_attribute_names_with_prefix(), and returned get_updated_html(). No _doing_it_wrong records.
Same documented and idiomatic pattern as the reference. The implementation avoids value parsing entirely, so boolean/empty/decoded attribute-value edge cases are not mishandled.
API usage is fully documented and appropriate. The function_exists wrapper is extra PHP structure but does not affect HTML API adherence or the hidden tests.

verdict.failure_analysis: All trials passed every hidden case: single-link, multiple-tags, multiple-matching-attributes, similar-prefixes-kept, uppercase-source-attribute, comments-untouched, and no-matches. There are no failed hidden cases to attribute to documentation gaps. The docs worked well here because the Tag Processor overview explicitly recommends it for flat attribute/class edits and byte-preserving output; the usage section shows direct construction with new WP_HTML_Tag_Processor; next_tag() documents walking all real tag openers while skipping comment text and incomplete tokens; get_attribute_names_with_prefix() documents lowercase returned names and case-insensitive matching; remove_attribute() supplies the needed mutation; and get_updated_html() is clearly presented as the retrieval method after queued edits. The main near-miss is that get_attribute_names_with_prefix() does not explicitly state the empty-array case for a matched tag with no matching attributes, though all candidates handled the nullable return safely anyway.

doc_gaps.problem: The return contract says array|null and shows null when no tag opener is matched, but it does not explicitly say that a matched tag with no matching attributes returns an empty array.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a sentence such as: "Returns an empty array when currently matched on a tag opener but no attribute name starts with the prefix; returns null only when no tag opener is currently matched."

doc_gaps.problem: The docs say returned names are lowercase, but they do not explicitly state that these normalized names are safe to pass back into get_attribute(), set_attribute(), or remove_attribute() to target source attributes with different original casing.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Document that returned names are comparable normalized names and may be passed directly to attribute APIs; matching remains ASCII case-insensitive for HTML attributes.

doc_gaps.problem: The method docblock is terse and does not surface useful removal semantics that matter for bulk attribute operations, including case-insensitive name matching, no-op behavior for absent attributes, duplicate-attribute removal, and whitespace preservation side effects.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Expand the contract to describe these general behaviors and point to get_updated_html() for byte-preserving output, noting that surrounding whitespace is not currently pruned.

trials.notes: Correctly used WP_HTML_Processor::create_fragment() for BODY-fragment normalization, walked tokens with next_token(), skipped SPAN tag tokens via get_tag(), and emitted serialize_token(). All called APIs are documented and no _doing_it_wrong records appeared. Minor risk: the get_last_error() fallback normalizes the original input, which would discard the rewrite if unsupported markup were encountered.

Correct processor and clean documented token-serialization pattern: create_fragment(), next_token(), get_tag(), serialize_token(). All APIs are documented and tests show no misuse. Minor omissions: raw-input fallback if processor creation fails, and no get_last_error() policy after a rewrite loop.

Uses the correct processor and only documented methods, with no _doing_it_wrong records. The failure is conceptual: it tracks SPAN depth and suppresses all tokens while inside a SPAN, which prunes the subtree instead of unwrapping boundary tag tokens. The docs' serialize_token() example shows skipping matching tag tokens while continuing to serialize descendants.

verdict.failure_analysis: Failed cases all come from trial-3. simple, attributes-discarded, adjacent-spans, span-with-block-content, and nested-spans fail because the candidate read “remove the element” as “remove the entire subtree”; its skip_span_depth gate drops text, IMG, EM, and nested SPAN contents. The relevant documentation is WP_HTML_Processor::serialize_token(), especially the “Remove every SUP element but keep its contents” example and the “rewrite while serializing tokens” recipe. Those passages were sufficient for trials 1 and 2, but the phrase “skip tokens to remove them” plus “Closing tokens of skipped elements must be skipped too” can still be misread as requiring a depth-based subtree skip. unclosed-span fails for the same reason: the processor normalizes the unclosed SPAN by visiting its text and virtual closers, but trial-3 suppresses the text while skip_span_depth is nonzero. The current_depth/is_tag_closer docs explain virtual closer and depth behavior, but the serialization docs do not explicitly warn that wrapper removal should keep serializing descendants even when the matching close tag has not yet been seen.

doc_gaps.location: WP_HTML_Processor::serialize_token() docblock and “Recipe: rewrite while serializing tokens”
doc_gaps.problem: The docs show a wrapper-removal example, but they do not explicitly distinguish omitting boundary tokens from pruning a whole subtree. A reader can over-apply depth state and drop descendants.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a short contract note: token rewrite loops operate on the current token only; to remove a wrapper, skip only the matching opener and closer tokens and continue serializing child tokens. To remove an element and all descendants, use a separate depth/breadcrumb-bounded subtree-pruning pattern.

doc_gaps.problem: Depth and breadcrumb examples are strong for subtree scans, but there is little guidance on when that state is inappropriate for flat token filters.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a cross-reference from subtree-walk examples to serialization rewrites: use depth/breadcrumb guards when the result depends on containment, but use a simple token predicate when every non-matching token should remain in output.

doc_gaps.location: WP_HTML_Processor::get_last_error() fallback guidance for serialization rewrites
doc_gaps.problem: Trials near-missed fallback behavior: normalizing the original input after a partial rewrite discards skipped or inserted tokens, and returning raw input is not normalized.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Make fallback policy examples more explicit: reject with null/empty string, return accumulated best-effort output, or normalize the original only when the caller explicitly accepts losing all rewrite changes.
